newsitem.title: USA: Dollar briefly spikes up on news of Deng's death.
newsitem.headline: Dollar briefly spikes up on news of Deng's death.

text.p: The dollar briefly spiked higher against the mark and rose to session highs against the yen on news of the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, dealers said.
However, the knee-jerk rise was short-lived and traders expect little further price action on the news that was widely anticipated.
"They were buying dollars and dollar/mark popped up past a resistance level at 1.70 marks, but it has come off since," said Doug Lee, assistant vice president at Sakura Bank Ltd.

The Hong Kong dollar and the Thailand bhat fell initially, said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank. He added that it could take some time for market players to calculate the long-term impact on the regional currencies.
The reaction in U.S. debt markets was muted as the news has no direct impact on the domestic economy, analysts said.

"I don't think it has any implications for U.S. or European markets. Even in the case of Pacific Rim markets, this news has been largely discounted over the last several years," said John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust.

"So while it causes a bit of uncertainty at the moment, I can't imagine anyone is shocked or surprised by this. If you use the old theory of buy the rumor, sell the fact, the flip side is now that the bad news is out, onward and upward for the markets," he added.
Rumors of Deng's death began to swirl in the currency market shortly after Hong-Kong based television station Chinese Television Network reported that Deng had died.
Within the hour, China's Xinhua news agency said the 93-year-old Deng died at 0808 EST/1308 GMT on Wednesday of complications from Parkinson's disease and a lung infection.
The announcement of Deng's death was made in a letter to the Communist Party, the People's Liberation Army and the people of various ethnic groups throughout China.

The dollar rose to a session high of 1.7005 marks on the rumors only to quickly return to its prior 1.6975 level by the time official word was released. Meanwhile, the dollar steadily inched higher against the yen until it hit a barrier at 124.40 yen, dealers said.

Traders said investors traditionally flock to dollars in times of political uncertainty and that the dollar exchange rate was more likely to be affected against the yen than against European currencies.
"Dollar/yen will be more affected due to the proximity and trade issues between the two nations, but any pressure on Asian currencies will be short-lived," said Lee at Sakura in New York.
In agreement with the relatively muted reaction in U.S. financial markets, U.S. government officials said that Deng's death will probably have little effect on the functioning of the country.
The 30-year U.S. Treasury long bond held steady, down 7/32 at 100.25/32 to yield 6.56 percent, in slow midafternoon activity.
